body_text: Why Manual Processes Are Unsustainable for Small Agencies July 02, 2026 by Shauna Seaver Government efficiency is often framed as a question of speed: faster approvals, less paperwork, or streamlined workflows. But in many public sector organizations, especially smaller districts and departments, the larger operational risk is dependency on manual processes. For SAU 14 Epping Schools in New Hampshire, that reality became difficult to sustain. Like many districts, Epping Schools operates with a lean administrative team responsible for finance, HR, payroll, compliance, transportation, and daily operations. Before modernizing many of their workflows, the district relied heavily on paper-based coordination and disconnected systems. As Business Administrator Christine Vayda described it, “The biggest thing that I saw is just recognizing the fact that the manual processes just weren’t sustainable.” When Manual Work Becomes an Operational Constraint In government organizations, inefficiency often comes from the accumulation of small administrative burdens: duplicate data entry, paper forms, delayed approvals, and staff spending time tracking information instead of acting on it. At Epping Schools, those burdens created delays across everyday operations. Leave requests moved between buildings before reaching the business office. Payroll and HR data required manual reconciliation. Contracts were mailed, signed physically, and returned through traditional routing processes. Budget reporting often depended on spreadsheets and separate systems that did not consistently align. Those inefficiencies become more significant in organizations with small teams and limited capacity. Across government, staff often spend significant time managing disconnects between systems rather than supporting higher-value work such as reporting, budgeting, and operational planning. Reducing Dependency Through Connected Systems Epping Schools’ modernization efforts focused on reducing operational friction across the organization. The district expanded their use of cloud-based HR, payroll, and finance systems to centralize operational workflows and improve visibility across departments. Approval workflows that once depended on paper routing were automated and became visible across departments. Employees gained self-service access to payroll information, contracts, leave requests, and onboarding materials. Administrators could review purchasing activity directly within the system rather than relying on manual handoffs between offices. The impact went beyond convenience. Contracts that previously took weeks to process through mail routing could now be completed electronically within hours. Financial records and invoices became searchable within the system rather than manually retrieved during audits. Personnel data flowed directly into budgeting and reporting processes, reducing the need for spreadsheet reconciliation and constant verification that information had been entered or calculated correctly. Epping Schools’ success highlights that the goal of efficiency is not simply reducing steps in a process. It is reducing how many routine operations depend on institutional memory, manual coordination, or individual intervention to function reliably. From Reactive Work to Proactive Operations Technology alone does not reduce operational dependency. Staff also need confidence in the processes being introduced. Vayda emphasized that modernization efforts succeeded because staff understood why the changes mattered, not just how the technology worked. Training and communication helped the team see how connected workflows reduced friction in their day-to-day tasks and supported a more proactive operating model. As Vayda described it, the goal was to create systems that “better supported our decision-making and allowed us to be a little more proactive instead of reactive.” Why Sustainability Matters More Than Speed Epping Schools’ experience reflects a broader challenge across government. The pursuit of operational efficiency must expand beyond completing work faster. It requires building operations that remain sustainable as staffing pressures, reporting demands, and service expectations continue to increase. The long-term value of modernization is creating resilient organizations that are less dependent on manual coordination, less vulnerable to operational bottlenecks, and better positioned to adapt as demands evolve. title: Summer Pet Safety Tips for Dogs and Cats
summary: Enjoy and learn from Life360's blog archive, focused on user life stories and experiences with our premier family safety app.
body_text: Summary What this article covers: A practical guide to summer pet safety tips for dogs and cats, covering heatstroke warning signs, hot pavement hazards, water and beach safety, fireworks prep, pest prevention, and how to respond when your pet needs help fast. Who it’s for Pet parents with dogs or cats who spend time outdoors in warm weather Families planning summer vacations, beach trips, or backyard gatherings with pets Anyone who wants to recognize heatstroke signs before they become an emergency Pet parents of brachycephalic breeds like Pugs, Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, or Persian cats Key Takeaways Dogs and cats cannot cool themselves the way humans do, making them far more vulnerable to heat than most pet parents realize Heatstroke can set in within 30 minutes in extreme heat and is a life-threatening emergency Hot pavement can burn your pet's paws well before it feels dangerous to you Fireworks aren't just loud — Life360's data shows over 75% of dogs feel it, and 22% try to run because of it A current ID and a real-time GPS tracker are the fastest way home if something goes wrong — Life360 pets wearing GPS reunite with their families in about 37 minutes on average Summer is the best time of year, until your dog is panting like a freight train at 10 a.m. and you realize the walk might have been a little ambitious. Warmer weather opens up a season of adventures for you and your pet, but these summer pet safety tips can help pet owners keep their furry friends and furry companions safe. The good news is that the vast majority of summer emergencies are preventable. You just need to know what to watch for, when to act, and how to set your pet up to thrive through every hot, humid, gloriously sunny week of it. Fireworks season is the riskiest week of the year for pets. Be ready. Life360 Pet GPS sends an instant escape alert the moment your pet leaves home — so you're searching in the right direction before they're even out of the neighborhood. See Life360 plans How Hot Weather Affects Your Pet's Body Here is the thing most pet parents don't fully appreciate until it matters: your dog and cat are working much harder than you are to stay cool. Dogs have sweat glands only on their paw pads, which means panting is their primary cooling mechanism. Cats groom themselves to spread moisture on their fur, which helps a little, but they rely heavily on shade and cool surfaces too. When the air around them is hot and humid, both methods lose effectiveness fast, and body temperature climbs quickly. A healthy pet's normal body temperature sits between 100 and 102.5 degrees Fahrenheit. Heat stroke sets in around 105 to 106 degrees, and at 108 degrees, organ damage can begin. In extreme heat, that escalation can happen in as little as 30 minutes. Certain pets are at even higher risk: brachycephalic breeds like Pugs, Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Boxers, and Persian cats have shortened airways that make efficient panting nearly impossible. Older pets, overweight animals, puppies, kittens, and those with heart or respiratory conditions also overheat faster than a healthy adult dog on a moderate day. Knowing your specific pet's risk level is one of the most practical things you can do before summer is fully underway. Signs of Heat Stroke to Watch For Catching heat-related illness early is the difference between a stressful afternoon and a genuine emergency. Early signs of heat stroke include excessive panting or drooling, bright red or dark gums, weakness, and stumbling. As the condition progresses, pets may vomit, develop bloody diarrhea, become confused or lethargic, and in severe cases, collapse or seize. If you see any of these warning signs of heat stroke, move your pet to a cool, shaded area immediately. Apply cool water (not ice cold) to the stomach, groin, and armpits. Offer small amounts of cool water and reintroduce water gradually if your pet is alert enough to drink. Then get to a veterinarian right away, even if your pet appears to stabilize. Internal damage from heat stroke is not always visible, and what looks like recovery can mask serious complications. Keep Activity Scheduled for Cooler Times The single most effective way to prevent heat-related illness is timing. The hottest part of the day typically runs from late morning through the mid-to-late afternoon, roughly 11 a.m. to 4 or 5 p.m. Schedule walks in the early morning or during the evening hours to avoid excessive heat and the day's high temperatures. Strenuous exercise should be avoided on days with high humidity, even if the temperature feels manageable, and during early summer when pets haven't yet adjusted to the season's higher temps. Shorter, shadier routes also help. Aim for grassy paths or tree-lined streets when you can. Always bring water and a collapsible bowl. Pets need frequent drink breaks during any outdoor activity in warm weather, not just when they look thirsty. Protect Your Pet's Paws from Hot Pavement Pavement absorbs heat and holds it well past when the sun goes down. On a day with an air temperature of 85 degrees, asphalt can reach surface temperatures of 135 degrees or higher. Your pet's paw pads can suffer burns quickly and with less drama than you'd expect. By the time your dog is limping, licking their feet, or refusing to walk, the damage is already done. The five-second rule is your most useful tool here: press the back of your hand flat on the pavement. If you cannot hold it there comfortably for five seconds, it is too hot for your dog's paws. Choose grass, dirt trails, or shaded sidewalks instead because hot asphalt and hot pavement can quickly burn your dog's paw pads. Protective booties designed for hot surfaces are another option for pet parents who need to stick to paved routes. Hydration and Water Safety Fresh water and clean water should be available at all times during the summer months. At home, keep multiple water bowls in cool spots and add ice cubes to help water stay cold longer. On outings, bring enough water for both of you and stop for breaks even if your pet hasn't asked. Pets won't always signal thirst clearly, especially when they're excited about being outside. A quick hydration check at home: gently lift the skin over your pet's shoulders. If it snaps back immediately, hydration is good. If it returns slowly or stays tented, your pet may be dehydrated and needs water and a cool spot right away. Near pools, lakes, and the beach, the risks shift. Not all dogs are strong swimmers, and even confident swimmers can tire quickly in open water or against a current. Introduce your pet to water gradually before any trip that involves swimming. Life jackets are essential on boats and paddleboards; if your dog falls off a paddleboard in open water, tipping the board trying to pull them back up is a real risk. Rinse your pet after any swim to remove chlorine, salt, or bacteria from their coat and paws, and never let your dog drink from the pool, ocean, or lake. Never Leave Your Pet in a Parked Car This one has no gray area. On an 85-degree day, the interior of a parked car can reach 100 degrees in under 10 minutes. Cracking the windows makes almost no difference. Shade helps very little. Cars trap and amplify heat faster than almost any other environment, and pets cannot escape from them. If you're running errands, your pet is safest at home in a cool space. If you travel with your pet frequently in warm weather, plan your stops around places where your pet can come with you or stay in a climate-controlled vehicle. Fireworks and the Runaway Report: What Life360's Data Actually Shows Dogs and cats hear at roughly four times the range humans do, so the booms and crackles of fireworks hit them a lot harder than most people realize. To find out exactly how much harder, Life360 dug into its own numbers for its first-ever Runaway Report: internal data from over 6 million pet profiles, our Pet GPS trackers, and our community-powered Pet Finder Network — plus a survey of 1,000 US dog parents. Here's the state of the escape: • Fireworks trigger an anxiety spike in over 75% of dogs in the US • 22% of dogs have bolted or attempted to escape their home specifically because of Fourth of July stress • One escape is rarely the last: 26% of runaway pets are repeat escapees • Middle-child dogs — not the youngest or oldest pet in the house — are 48% more likely to run • The witching hour is real: most runaways happen between 3 and 6 p.m. local time • Los Angeles, Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Atlanta, and Chicago top the list for escape artists • Dobermans, Huskies, Chihuahuas, and Pitbulls trigger the most Lost Pet Alerts on Life360; Retrievers, Pomeranians, Border Collies, and Boxers trigger the fewest Pet parents feel it too. Nearly half worry their dog could run during a fireworks-heavy holiday, and half report rising anxiety as the celebrations approach. If their dog actually went missing mid-fireworks, 65% say they'd be highly stressed — 35% admit they'd go straight into panic mode. Yet only 37% feel very confident they could recall their dog successfully if they escaped. “Living in a rural area surrounded by woods and open land, we've relied on Life360's Pet GPS tracker more than once to quickly locate our dog on the map. She's been known to bolt when startled by loud noises. It even once found our cat after her tracker's battery had run out and switched to Bluetooth mode. The biggest benefit is knowing that if something happens, we're not left guessing where our pets are. It's a simple tool that can take away a lot of stress and has given our family incredible peace of mind.” — Ashley Jordan, Life360 member It's no surprise, then, that the Fourth of July is quietly becoming a stay-home holiday for a lot of pet parents. Over half (51%) now spend the evening in with their dog instead of heading out, and more than 40% say they've skipped a holiday gathering entirely to keep their pet safe and comfortable — one in five of that group has done it more than once. Life360's Pet Parenthood Report backs this up: Pet owners check on their animals in the app slightly more often than their human kids (a median of 15 times a month versus 13). Fireworks season might be the clearest proof yet of how far people will go for their furry family members. Real-Time Tracking When Your Pet Needs It Most Prevention comes first, but when a pet does get out, every minute counts — and that's where a digital safety net changes the outcome. GPS tracking ranks as pet parents' number one reunification tool: more than 90% trust it, and 54% say it's the one tool they'd trust most if their dog ran off. Here's the number that matters most: pets wearing a Life360 Pet GPS reunite with their families in about 37 minutes on average. That's the difference between a scare and a tragedy. And if your pet does go missing, the Lost Pet Alert taps into our community-powered Pet Finder Network of over 100 million members, putting more eyes on the search than you could ever manage alone. Make sure your pet's collar has a current ID tag with your phone number, and keep microchip registration current with your address and contact info — do this now, before the next big holiday weekend, not after. title: Antidepressant Sexual Dysfunction and Women's Health with Anita Clayton, MD
summary: Anita Clayton, MD, built the scale for measuring antidepressant sexual dysfunction. She made psychiatry pay attention to women's sexcual health, and was featured in the documentary "The Little Pink Pill." Learn to tell disease, medication, and relationship causes apart.
body_text: The short answer: After noticing fluoxetine's label listed it at under 2% while she saw roughly 20% in clinic, she built the Changes in Sexual Functioning Questionnaire (CSFQ), the validated scale now used in drug trials across many specialties. Dr. Anita Clayton, chair of psychiatry at UVA and a former Navy physician, is one of the people most responsible for medicine measuring antidepressant sexual dysfunction. Takeaways: Why drug labels understate antidepressant sexual side effects, and why spontaneous-report data misses what a validated scale catches. The three kinds of sexual dysfunction clinicians should separate: disease-state, treatment-emergent, and relationship-based. Which antidepressants carry low sexual-side-effect risk, including bupropion and gepirone ER (Exxua), the 2023-approved drug with no sexual-dysfunction label warning. The FDA double standard Dr. Clayton fought during the flibanserin (Addyi) approval, where "successful sexual events" was the benchmark borrowed from Viagra trials. The faster-acting depression treatments she's studying now, including zuranolone and a single-dose psilocybin-analog injectable for postpartum depression. The package insert for fluoxetine said 1.9% of patients experienced sexual dysfunction. Dr. Anita Clayton was a Navy psychiatrist in the early 1990s, putting most of her patients on the drug because it was safer in overdose than the tricyclics she'd watched kill people. Her patients, mostly Navy sailors and Marines, kept telling her the same thing: it was taking a lot longer to reach orgasm. She checked the label. It said under 2%. What she was seeing in clinic was at least 20%. So she built the tool to prove it: the Changes in Sexual Functioning Questionnaire, the CSFQ, now used in drug trials across psychiatry, cardiology, and neurology. On this episode of Psychiatry Tomorrow, Osmind Chief Medical Officer Dr. Will Sauvé and co-host Dr. Brittany Albright sit down with Dr. Clayton, chair of psychiatry at the University of Virginia, a former Navy physician, and a past president of the International Society for the Study of Women's Sexual Health. She's spent her career insisting women's sexual health was real, measurable, and treatable — a fight documented in the film The Pink Pill: Sex, Drugs and Who Has Control (2025) on Paramount+, in which she appears. This conversation traces how she got there, starting years before fluoxetine. Treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction is sexual dysfunction caused by a medication rather than by the underlying illness. It can appear in a patient who had no sexual problems before starting the drug, which is why it has to be measured against a baseline rather than assumed from a patient's spontaneous report. How did a nursing-home visit set Dr. Clayton on the path to medicine? Clayton knew she wanted to be a doctor at five years old, after a childhood spent visiting a grandmother in a Mobile, Alabama nursing home. Her mother made the visits long on purpose, stopping to talk with every resident before they ever reached her grandmother's room. One day, young Anita asked who took care of all these people. Her mother said, the doctors. "Well, then I guess I wanna be one," she decided. Surgery was her first rotation at UVA, where she excelled but knew she didn't want to be a surgeon. Pediatrics didn't fit either. She joked she wanted a Valium dispenser at the clinic door for the terrified parents. OB-GYN and psychiatry were the two that stuck, for the same reason: both let her into people's lives at the most intimate level. OB-GYN is intimate the way psychiatry is intimate, Clayton says, only physically rather than emotionally. As Sauvé remembers it, a classmate put it even more bluntly back in medical school: he'd wanted to be a psychiatrist because, in his words, "it's the most invasive specialty there is." What two years as the Navy “country doctor” taught her about treating the whole person The Navy paid for Clayton's medical school, which meant two years owed as a general medical officer at Great Lakes Naval Hospital, the "country doctor" stretch military physicians do before specialty training. She pulled her one year of psychiatry training straight into primary care and started a women's group with a Navy psychologist: five minutes for physical complaints, then the real conversation about what was going on in their lives. It caught real diagnoses: a likely case of giardia, a patient whose seizures tracked to medication non-compliance after fights with her husband. She kept finding things other providers missed, until radiology called to complain. "You send more people up here, and we find more things than everyone else in the hospital combined," they told her. Her answer: "Well, I'm examining them." The group had an unplanned ending: one member ran hiring at a local Kmart and offered the others jobs. They took them, and started skipping sessions to go to work instead. Clayton never had to tell anyone they were done. As Sauvé put it, the best possible reason to skip the psychiatrist is that you're too busy living your life. How common is sexual dysfunction with antidepressants, really? "It's at least 20% from what I'm seeing," Clayton remembers thinking, after checking fluoxetine's label and finding 1.9%. Albright named the lesson directly: "We can't always trust the PI, the package insert, when it comes to sexual side effects." The gap exists because label numbers come from spontaneous reports, patients volunteering information unprompted, which almost nobody does about sex. What you actually want is a scale that measures change from a baseline. There wasn't a good one, so Clayton built one after returning to UVA, using medical students as her general population sample. She set the CSFQ's cutoff scores where the confidence intervals didn't overlap. The scale has since been used well beyond psychiatry: cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurological disorders. The three kinds of sexual dysfunction clinicians confuse Depression itself causes sexual dysfunction, and treating it can help. But the treatment can also cause it: a patient with no sexual problems going in can develop them on the medication. A third source is the relationship itself, shaped by the social withdrawal that depression brings. Each of the three calls for a different response, which makes telling them apart the first clinical task. Which antidepressants don't cause sexual dysfunction? Clayton's studies showed bupropion, which came to market around the same time as fluoxetine, didn't cause sexual dysfunction, and that adding it can rescue sexual function lost to an SSRI. She took that finding to industry, and ran into a wall: companies were fixated on being a first-line treatment. "What do you care if you're a first-line treatment or second-line treatment, or you're added in as a second drug?" she told them. "It's a prescription. Just count the prescriptions." Stop thinking of these as only antidepressants, she argued. They're potentially anti-sexual dysfunction drugs. Why was flibanserin (Addyi), the drug at the center of The Pink Pill, approved only after a decade-long fight with the FDA? The Pink Pill (2025) , in which Clayton appears, flibanserin is the subject that eventually becomes approved as Addyi. Boehringer Ingelheim first tested it as an antidepressant, where it didn't separate from placebo. It turned out to affect the sexual dysfunction wrapped up in depression. Clayton was part of the research from the start. The drug caused sedation, so dosing moved to nighttime, and regulators still worried about mothers falling asleep at the wheel the next morning. Clayton calls it "really prudish." The deeper absurdity was in how the FDA wanted desire measured: for men, with Viagra, the bar had been "successful sexual events," whether the penis was firm enough for penetration, nothing about orgasm or satisfaction. "Have you ever talked to a woman and asked her if she's had a successful sexual event?" Clayton said. "Maybe satisfying, but successful? No." They eventually agreed to change the word to "satisfying," which she still found absurd. "Why don't you ask them about their desire? You think they forget?" Boehringer Ingelheim eventually gave up on the drug. It was in-licensed by Cindy and Bob Whitehead's company Sprout, which ran the studies needed for approval. Women from those trials testified at FDA meetings about what the treatment had done for them. Addyi was approved in 2015. Fast-acting mechanisms for postpartum depression, and a single-dose psilocybin analog Clayton moved from reproductive psychiatry into PMDD and postpartum depression, chasing what she calls the newest possible mechanisms. She ran trials on Zuranolone, an allopregnanolone analog that works fast at GABA receptors and uses a short dosing course instead of a daily pill. She's now studying a psilocybin-analog injectable for postpartum depression, a shorter-acting metabolite needing far less monitoring than psilocybin, given as a single dose. The FDA required an active very-low-dose comparator instead of placebo, to avoid unblinding patients. She describes the postpartum results as significantly positive, with the paper in progress, and the same compound is now being studied in adjustment disorder tied to serious illness: cancer, Parkinson's, MS, ALS, interstitial lung disease. Albright spoke about rapid acting treatments already in use for one such patient, treated for ALS with a full course of Spravato and TMS: "The month before he died, he told me he was happy, and he felt at peace, and that was the best gift." And then there's a drug that closes the loop back to sexual dysfunction specifically: gepirone ER, sold as Exxua, the first oral selective 5-HT1A agonist for major depression, approved in 2023, with a label that carries no sexual-dysfunction warning because trials showed no difference from placebo on that measure. To prove it, the studies compared the drug head-to-head against an SSRI in people who didn't have depression, isolating the medication's effect on sexual function without depression itself muddying the results. Mentorship, and staying curious Clayton didn't have mentors for clinical research at UVA, so she found her own, reaching out to researchers whose papers she'd read and asking them to supervise her remotely. They were all men, and all said yes. "They just said, 'Yes, you can do it. I'll help you,'" she said. Not, "'This is such a burden... this is gonna be so hard.' None of it." Both she and Albright trace that support back further. Clayton's father, a Navy pilot, told his two daughters: "You can do anything you want. And you should believe that." Asked what she's proudest of, Clayton didn't name an accomplishment. She named a disposition. "I'm still excited," she said. "And I think I will be for a very long time." ‍ ‍ Frequently asked questions about antidepressant sexual dysfunction How common is sexual dysfunction with antidepressants? Sexual dysfunction with antidepressants is far more common than older drug labels suggested. Dr. Anita Clayton notes that fluoxetine's package insert once listed it at about 1.9%, while she was observing roughly 20% in clinical practice. The gap exists because label figures often come from spontaneous patient reports rather than studies that measure sexual function with a validated scale, and most patients do not bring up sexual side effects on their own. What are the three types of sexual dysfunction clinicians should distinguish? Dr. Clayton describes three sources of sexual dysfunction that clinicians should tell apart: disease-state dysfunction caused by the depression itself, treatment-emergent dysfunction caused by a medication such as an SSRI, and relationship-based dysfunction shaped by the social withdrawal that comes with depression. Sorting out which one is driving a patient's symptoms comes first, before deciding how to address it. Which antidepressants are least likely to cause sexual dysfunction? Several antidepressants are associated with low rates of sexual dysfunction. Dr. Clayton's research showed bupropion did not cause it, and adding low-dose bupropion can help with SSRI-related sexual side effects. Gepirone ER (Exxua), approved in 2023 as the first oral selective 5-HT1A agonist for major depression, carries no sexual-dysfunction warning on its label because it did not differ from placebo on that measure in trials. What is flibanserin (Addyi) and what is it used for? Flibanserin, marketed as Addyi, was approved by the FDA in 2015 as the first medication for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women. It is a serotonin 1A receptor agonist and 2A antagonist that was originally tested as an antidepressant. Dr. Clayton, who was involved in the research from the start, describes a long and contested approval process documented in the film The Pink Pill. Are there fast-acting treatments for postpartum depression? Yes, newer options work faster than traditional oral antidepressants. Dr. Clayton ran trials on zuranolone, an allopregnanolone analog that acts at GABA, works quickly, and uses a short dosing course rather than a daily pill. She is also studying a single-dose psilocybin-analog injectable for postpartum depression that requires less monitoring than psilocybin itself, with results she describes as significantly positive and a paper in progress. Clinical note: This article summarizes a clinical conversation for educational purposes and is not medical advice. Descriptions of investigational treatments and trials reflect Dr. Clayton's own account of work in progress; some results she references are not yet published and have not been independently verified here. FDA approval status, indications, and labeling for the medications named can change. Clinicians should base treatment decisions on current prescribing information, individual patient assessment, and applicable regulatory guidance. Sources and notes Clayton AH, McGarvey EL, Clavet GJ. body_text: At Novo Nordisk, our priority is patients — especially those living with diabetes and obesity who still lack access to effective treatment.
